name: Redpanda
workload: OpenMessaging-Benchmark-based test at three sustained throughput levels (50 MB/s, 500 MB/s, 1 GB/s) with a 1:1 read/write ratio and 4 partitions/core, comparing p99.99 tail latency on AWS instances
hardware: AWS: 4x m5n.8xlarge clients (128GB RAM, 32 vCPU); servers varied by workload: i3en.large / is4gen.medium (small), i3en.3xlarge (medium), i3en.6xlarge (large)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running Redpanda as a competing hosted service (source-available, not OSI-approved); benchmark hardware given as AWS instance families rather than exact CPU model
caveats: First-party blog benchmark; uses a modified version of the OpenMessaging Benchmark that is not itself linked; compiler/build flags not stated; only instance types (not CPU model/stepping) given for hardware
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than Kafka" -> HN Algolia query "redpanda kafka benchmark" -> redpanda.com/blog/redpanda-vs-kafka-performance-benchmark

name: TCPSHM
workload: Echo client/server round-trip-time benchmark on the same host, variable message sizes randomly chosen from (16, 36, 68, 200) bytes
claimed_speedup: TCP mode RTT 8.818us vs ZeroMQ TCP REQ/REP 42.268us (~4.8x); SHM mode RTT 0.338us vs ZeroMQ IPC (Unix domain socket) 30.653us (~91x)
hardware: Ubuntu 14.04, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.10GHz, cpupin enabled on both client and server
tradeoffs: Header-only, no disk persistence, non-blocking busy-poll design raises CPU usage, degrades past ~1000 live connections, single-writer-thread-per-connection constraint, message length capped at uint16_t
caveats: Compiler and optimization flags not stated; same-host loopback test only, not a networked/distributed comparison; project inactive since 2020
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than ZeroMQ"

name: Wisp
workload: NATS-Core-wire-protocol pub/sub fan-out: 1 publisher, 1,000 subscribers, 128-byte payloads, 100,000 publications (=100M aggregate deliveries per run), 3 repeated runs, CPU-pinned client/server
claimed_speedup: 4.37x higher median aggregate delivery throughput than NATS 2.14.6 (9,023,597 vs 2,066,099 deliveries/sec); 76.4% less server CPU time
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --locked (Rust 2024-edition toolchain; exact rustc version not pinned in the artifacts)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 9700X; server pinned to CPUs 0-3,8-11, client pinned to 4-7,12-15 (4 physical cores/8 logical CPUs each)
tradeoffs: Experimental single-author project; not a full NATS Core replacement (no clustering, JetStream, or persistence); comparison is same-host loopback, not over a real network
caveats: Very new/low-visibility repo (2 stars, no LICENSE file so the code cannot legally be reused); exact rustc/toolchain version is not pinned even though build flags, CPU model and affinity are documented in detail; single-host measurement
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than NATS"

name: FluxMQ
workload: Kafka-wire-protocol-compatible broker throughput/latency test using Java Kafka client tooling; exact record size/partition count not documented
claimed_speedup: 476K msg/sec average (28.6% faster than Kafka's stated 370K msg/sec), 554K msg/sec peak (49.6% faster); 0.002ms vs 0.003ms average latency (33% lower)
compiler_and_flags: RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", cargo build --release (from install instructions; not confirmed as the exact flags used for the cited benchmark numbers)
tradeoffs: Single binary, no ZooKeeper/JVM dependency; Kafka protocol compatibility is partial (20 APIs implemented); very young, low-adoption project with placeholder repo URL fields in its own README
caveats: No CPU/hardware model stated for the cited numbers; heavily marketing-styled README with emoji scorecards; Kafka version, tuning, and dataset used for the comparison are undocumented; treat as an unverified first-party claim
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than Kafka"

name: SocketPro
workload: Persistent message queue comparison between SocketPro and RabbitMQ/Kafka; benchmark driver scripts for Kafka (kafka_perf_test.txt) and a rabbitmq/ sample dir exist in-repo, but no results data or hardware description is checked in
claimed_speedup: "SocketPro could be 50 times faster than RabbitMQ"; separately claims to be "significantly faster" than Kafka with no numbers given
tradeoffs: No license file (cannot legally reuse the code as-is); low adoption; the vendor's own detailed-results page (udaparts.com) is no longer reachable (DNS failure at time of research)
caveats: The only numeric claim (50x vs RabbitMQ) is for a baseline outside Kafka/NATS/ZeroMQ; the Kafka claim has no number; primary evidence page is dead; in-repo benchmark scripts exist but no committed results/hardware info to verify against
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than Kafka" (udaparts/socketpro:samples/qperf/README.md)

name: Zenoh
workload: Independent NTU-team evaluation: single-machine and 100Gb-Ethernet multi-machine pub/sub throughput sweep across payload sizes 8B-512MB, comparing Zenoh 0.7.0-rc (peer & brokered modes), Apache Kafka 3.2.1 (rdkafka 0.28.0 client), Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0.15 (MQTT), and Cyclone DDS
claimed_speedup: Zenoh peer mode: 65x higher bitrate than Kafka at 8B payload, ~24x at its 8KB throughput peak, ~10x at 32KB (single-machine scenario, derived from page data for some ratios)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X fixed at 4.0GHz (8-core/16-thread), 32GB DDR4-3200MHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario over 100Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: Evaluation used Zenoh 0.7.0-rc, a 2023 pre-release version; the rdkafka Kafka bindings used failed to send messages above 1MB, limiting the comparison at large payload sizes; benchmark exercised the Rust zenoh core, not the official zenoh-c/zenoh-cpp C/C++ bindings directly (though they wrap the same core)
caveats: Contributed by an academic team (National Taiwan University) but published on Zenoh's own blog in collaboration with ZettaScaleLabs (Zenoh's commercial backer), so not fully arm's-length independent; exact compiler versions for each system under test are not stated, though component/library versions are precisely pinned; benchmark code is public at github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf (not opened this session, so not cited as the benchmark_url) and a fuller arXiv writeup (2303.09419) exists but was not opened this session

name: Woodpecker
workload: Single-node, single-client, single-log-stream write-ahead-log throughput/latency test comparing Woodpecker (local filesystem, S3, and MinIO backends) against Kafka and Pulsar
claimed_speedup: Local-FS mode: 450 MB/s vs Kafka's 129.96 MB/s (3.5x) and Pulsar's 107 MB/s (4.2x), with 1.8ms vs Kafka's 58ms latency; S3 mode: 750 MB/s (5.8x vs Kafka)
tradeoffs: Purpose-built as Milvus's write-ahead-log layer rather than a general-purpose broker; local-FS/S3/MinIO modes trade off durability and availability differently; project explicitly describes results as "early stages of development"
caveats: First-party benchmark from the Milvus/Zilliz docs; no CPU/hardware model stated ("our test machine"); Kafka/Pulsar tuning and dataset are undocumented; single-node/single-stream test, not a distributed cluster comparison
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than Kafka"
